summary: The cupbearer sees a vine put out branches, blossom and bear ripe grapes. Israel can itself be pictured as a vine brought out of Egypt and planted in the land. In John, Jesus calls himself the vine and his disciples the branches.

senses.definition: The plant whose clusters yield grapes and wine. Its wood, leaves and fruit may each be in view.

evidence.note: Three branches bud and blossom, and their clusters ripen into grapes.
The Nazirite abstains from everything produced by the wine vine.
Ezekiel asks what use the wood of a vine has among the trees.

senses.definition: A vine beside a fig tree pictures the settled enjoyment of the land and its produce.

evidence.note: Each sits under his vine and fig tree with no one to frighten him.
The Assyrian envoy promises each man the fruit of his own vine.

senses.gloss: vine as an image of a person or people
senses.definition: The planting, spreading and fruitfulness of a vine describe people and their fortunes.

evidence.note: God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it after driving out nations.
Israel is called a vine that bears fruit.
In the eagle riddle the seed grows into a low, spreading vine.
The wife is compared to a fruitful vine.

senses.definition: A trailing field plant from which a gatherer took wild gourds.

evidence.note: The gatherer cuts its unfamiliar fruits into the stew.

senses.definition: The vine bears fruit and supports the branches from which the fruit grows.

evidence.note: A detached branch cannot bear fruit.

senses.definition: Jesus describes his disciples as branches whose fruit depends on their remaining in him.

evidence.note: Jesus identifies himself as the true vine and his Father as the cultivator.

cognates.note: This form retains the n. The Peshitta noun below has a feminine ending.
The Akkadian glossary gives a broader plant term. Its attested glosses here do not identify a grapevine.

note: The fruit in 2Ki 4:39 is called wild gourds. The verse supports a field vine but leaves its precise botanical identity uncertain. No verse requires the broad Akkadian sense ‘bush’ for the Hebrew. The Peshitta word is SEDRA lexeme 619.
